Conic Sections

CurvesGeometryCoordinates
Game: This shows the shape you get when a flat sheet cuts through a double cone.
How to play: Drag the dot on the tilt arc or slide the dot on the cone's middle line. You can also use the sliders or press a shape button.
25.0° 7.0
Look for the math

A tilted sheet can cut a cone in several different curves. The surprise is that only two angles decide which one you get, and that the cut through the vertex is a smaller, sharper version of the same answer.

The two angles on the page

The original applet's page calls them α, the angle a line on the cone makes with its base, and β, the angle the cutting plane makes with that base. Both are acute; β may be zero. In the applet's own geometry the cone has radius 6 and height 12, so tan(α) = 12/6 = 2 and α ≈ 63.435°. This port keeps that cone and moves only the plane, so the tilt arc covers 0° ≤ β ≤ 80° and crosses α.

The page's claim, checked in the logic test over every whole degree and many random ones, is:

β < α → ellipse (or a point at the vertex)
β = α → parabola (or one line at the vertex)
β > α → hyperbola (or two lines at the vertex)
β = 0 → the ellipse is a circle

These are the four conic sections named on the page. Every one of the claims holds for the acute angles the applet allows.

Why the comparison works

Put the cone's vertex at the origin and its axis along x. A double cone of radius 6 and height 12 is y² + z² = m² x² with m = 6/12 = cot(α). A plane tilted by β is x − y tan(β) = d, where d is where it crosses the axis. Using coordinates (u, v) inside the plane turns the cut into

A u² + B u + C + v² = 0
A = cos²(β) − m² sin²(β)

The sign of A alone decides the shape: it is positive exactly when tan(β) < 1/m = tan(α). Positive gives an ellipse, zero gives a parabola, negative gives a hyperbola. At β = 0 the two half-widths of the ellipse are both |d| m, so it is a circle, just as the page says.

What happens at the vertex

When the plane passes through the vertex, d = 0 and the whole curve shrinks onto that point. The logic test checks the three cases: a point when β < α, one line when β = α (the plane lies along a generator), and a pair of lines when β > α. Move the plane dot onto the black vertex to see them; move it away again and the curve opens out.

What changed from the Java applet

The original was a Java 3D scene: you rotated, slid and zoomed a finite cone and a square translucent plane with the mouse, with radio buttons for separate or combined motion and transparent or opaque plane. It never named the curve. This port shows the same geometry as a flat side view plus the cut seen face-on, with two draggable dots and sliders in place of the mouse gestures; the two radio choices are the two toggle buttons. The cone keeps the applet's 6 by 12 shape, so the angle comparison above is the page's, not a new rule.

Try Circle, then Ellipse, then Parabola and Hyperbola in that order. Watch what happens as the tilt passes the generator angle, then press Through the vertex.
